newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland's frontline kids find rural solace.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland's frontline kids find rural solace.

text.p: For the children of Belfast caught up in Northern Ireland's latest eruption of violence, Glebe House offers something they cannot find among the broken glass and burned out cars.

Located deep in the green South Down countryside, with donkeys and goats in nearby fields, the house is a haven for youngsters from both sides of the troubled province's sectarian and political divide.

Just as London children were sent to the country to escape World War Two bombs, Belfast is sending many of its youngsters away from the unrest that followed last Sunday's march by Protestant Orangemen through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Television screens have been filled with images of masked teenagers throwing petrol bombs at police and soldiers. But many inner city parents want their children to have no part in the mayhem.

This weekend, as the annual Orange Order "marching season" reaches its height, staff at Glebe House are facing such heavy demand from anxious Belfast parents that they have had to hire extra space in another building nearby.
"There's a lot of violence and conflict," Glebe House manager Diarmaid McGarrigle told Reuters. "A lot of parents are very worried."
But this being Northern Ireland, the parents are not just worried about what might happen to their children in street riots.
There is also great sensitivity about being seen to allow them to mix with children on the other side of the religious divide.

"The programmes are primarily organised to bring children from both sides of the community togther, so they can get to meet each other and get to understand some of the differences there are perceived to be between them," McGarrigle said.
For many of the children from Belfast's working class inner city areas it will be the first time they have been to the country and seen farm animals.

And although they may live only a short distance from each other in Belfast's Catholic and Protestant strongholds, the childrens' visit to Glebe House may be the first time they actually get to spend any length of time with each other.
"If the children raise topics of concern, we try to act on them right away," McGarrigle said.
"If they come out with statements which are incorrect or sectarian, we deal with them. We don't let anybody get away with anything that is total nonsense."

Glebe House is charity which takes children aged between seven and 16 for stays of about 10 days. It is expecting about 30 from Belfast this weekend as concern grows over Saturday's Orange Order march down the Catholic Lower Ormeau Road.
